title: Enterprise on-Prem Trust Claim Messaging — Regulated Workloads
purpose: Create a concise, audit-forward set of messaging claims and seller rebuttals that field teams can use when engaging compliance-heavy buyers evaluating private (VPC/on-prem) deployment of Redwood's control plane.
audience: Sales reps, solutions engineers, CSMs; secondary: product marketing and legal for rapid review cycles.
one_liner: We give regulated teams a verifiable, end-to-end evidence kit that proves customer control over data, keys, and audit records while keeping the same developer ergonomics as our hosted API.
lead_messages: Control plane sovereignty: the customer's control plane (VPC or on-prem) holds audit logs, keys, and policy enforcement — Redwood's control plane provides orchestration only.
Composable evidence: prebuilt artifacts (config templates, audit samples, SOC-like checklists) accelerate audits and reduce cycle time for procurement and security reviews.
Fallback resiliency: automated policy-based fallbacks keep apps running on vetted hosted or dedicated model variants while preserving data controls and SLOs.
Engineer-first UX: same SDK/endpoint model; teams can iterate locally and then pin a deployment mode for production without rewriting code.
Cost vs risk framing: upfront pilot investment is paid back by reduced audit cycles, lower integration cost, and simplified SLA mapping compared to homegrown stacks.
detailed_talking_points: Use this section as the seller script for discovery calls and security deep dives. Start with binding statements (what the customer controls) and then walk through the evidence kit. Sections: (1) What you truly control — keys, IAM, logs, VPC routing, and storage lifetime. (2) Where Redwood acts only as a managed operator — model artifacts/runtime templates; we never have access to customer KMS keys in control-plane mode. (3) Audit artifacts we provide: sample SIEM forwarders, schema for immutable audit events, a snapshot of access logs, and a mapping of Redwood telemetry to common frameworks (SOC2, ISO27001 controls). Always offer the evidence kit before technical deep dives — it short-circuits many objections.
buyer_objections: We can't trust an external company to run any part of our control plane.
We need air-gapped/offline deployment; cloud UI or telemetry is a non-starter.
How do we prove chain-of-custody for data going into a model?
What if you later change the control plane to an operator-managed model?
This sounds expensive compared to self-hosting open-source runtimes.
rebuttals_and_evidence: Sovereignty rebuttal: In our VPC/on-prem model the customer owns the control plane VPC and all network policies. Redwood's control plane services are deployed into customer-controlled subnets or on-prem infrastructure; we provide a signed architecture diagram and deployment provenance for legal review.

Air-gap rebuttal: We support an air-gapped bundle and an on-prem-only control plane distribution; during pilots we can run an offline install with a pre-signed manifest and an HSM/KMS integration checklist.

Chain-of-custody rebuttal: We supply sample immutable logs (signed events), a recommended retention policy, and a deterministic mapping layer that records model inputs, model version, and policy decisions for replay and forensic review.

Operator-change rebuttal: Customers can pin runtime images and model versions. We document upgrade policies and maintain rolling rollback artifacts; contractual SLA terms can be added to restrict unilateral control-plane changes.

TCO rebuttal: Provide a side-by-side pilot budget: support and maintenance overhead for a self-hosted solution vs Redwood private deployment including evidence-prep time — highlight audit-hours saved and faster procurement closure as line items.
competitor_differentiators: Versus managed cloud AI endpoints: we minimize external plane access and provide an evidence bundle specifically tailored for audits (not just a product sheet).

Versus pure open-source stacks: we deliver packaged operational artifacts (auditable manifests, signed logs, KMS integrations, upgrade rollbacks) so teams don't rebuild operational runbooks from scratch.
Versus other vendors offering 'self-managed control planes': our UX keeps dev-tooling identical to hosted mode so app velocity isn't sacrificed for compliance.
evidence_kit_inventory: Signed deployment manifest (SHA256) and provenance readme
Sample immutable audit event stream (jsonl) with schema mapping
KMS/HSM integration template and sample CMK rotation policy
Network diagram with subnet, flow logs, and recommended ACL rules
Compliance checklist mapped to SOC2/ISO controls and typical procurement questions
pilot_ask_and_success_criteria: 30-day technical pilot: deploy control plane bundle into customer VPC or air-gapped environment, ingest 1–2 internal apps, validate audit exports to customer's SIEM.
Success signals: SIEM ingestion verified, keys managed by customer KMS, sample audit replay executed by customer's security team, developer feedback on parity with hosted API.
Typical pilot scope: 2 engineers from customer + 1 SE + 1 infra PM from Redwood. Expected calendar time: 6–8 sprints of validation and artifact handoff.
next_steps: Attach evidence kit to initial NDA and offer architecture working session.
Prepare a customized evidence checklist for procurement and legal; request customer's compliance questionnaire in advance.
If the buyer is C-level focused: prepare a one-page risk reduction and TCO slide for exec review (include expected audit-hours saved).
content: Notes to seller: Keep language concrete. Security teams respond to artifacts, not promises. When asked for assurances, default to offering the evidence kit and a short architecture workshop. If the buyer is most worried about data-in-motion, show the network diagram and flow logs example first. If they are worried about legal exposure, pull the CMK rotation and retention artifacts. Add any new customer Qs into the shared thread so we can iterate on the evidence kit. -- End of brief
